clue.text: Bound to move sharply to get car moving

blocks.note: to bound is to leap
to start is to make a sudden jerk, as when surprised

explanation.surface: An instruction to leap and dart about in order to get a stalled car going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound to' looks like 'obliged to', but Bound is a verb of its own here.
explanation.definitionFit: To jump-start a vehicle is to start its engine using cables from another battery, which gets the stalled vehicle going.

clue.text: Poke centre of knotty lace frill

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle, so only the two central letters are kept

blocks.note: a jab is a quick poke
the middle two letters of knotty

explanation.surface: Someone prods at the tangled middle of a lace ruffle.
explanation.definitionFit: A jabot is an ornamental frill of lace or cloth worn on the front of a shirt or blouse.

clue.text: Huge unhappy moans from one with grave commission

indicators.note: something unhappy is out of sorts, so the letters of the next word are out of order

blocks.note: monumental means enormous
letters of moans rearranged

explanation.surface: Loud complaints come from someone entrusted with a serious task.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grave' looks like 'serious' but means a burial grave.
explanation.definitionFit: A monumental mason carves headstones and memorials, so their commissions are literally for graves.

clue.text: Firm dates rescheduled quickly

indicators.note: rescheduling puts things into a new order, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: letters of dates rearranged
fast means quickly

explanation.surface: A company moves its appointments at short notice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' looks like a business, but it is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Steadfast describes someone resolutely unwavering in purpose or loyalty, as a firm friend or firm resolve is.

clue.text: A phoney with bleeding heart smitten by conscience

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its middle, so the central letters are kept

blocks.note: taken as written
a sham is a fake or phoney
the middle two letters of bleeding

explanation.surface: A fraud with a bleeding heart is struck with guilt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bleeding heart' reads as a soft-hearted person; here it simply means the middle of bleeding.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling ashamed means being troubled by guilt or embarrassment over one's own conduct.

clue.text: Window over door takes time and huge price

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
'a king's ransom' is a huge price

explanation.surface: A window over the door takes ages to fit and costs a fortune.
explanation.definitionFit: A transom window is the small window set above a door, often called a fanlight in Britain.

clue.text: Muslim lady takes ends of brittle stick

indicators.note: the ends of a word are its first and last letters, so only those two are kept

blocks.note: the first and last letters of brittle
to gum is to stick with glue

explanation.surface: A woman snaps a brittle stick in two and takes the ends.
explanation.definitionFit: Begum is a title of rank for a high-born Muslim woman in South Asia, roughly equal to a lady.

clue.text: Label chimney as one to pour out smoke inwardly

indicators.note: inwardly means on the inside, so the letters lie within the words given

blocks.note: spans the end of Label and the start of chimney

explanation.surface: A chimney is tagged as the source of the smoke.
explanation.definitionFit: Chimneys and factories are said to belch smoke when they emit thick clouds of it forcefully.

clue.text: No place for private patients?

blocks.note: surface reading: an NHS ward that does not take fee-paying patients
setter's reading: a private is the lowest army rank, and a senior officer is no place for one

explanation.walkthrough: The answer's first word is an army rank far above a private soldier, while the whole phrase is a public hospital rather than a private one.
explanation.definitionFit: A state-run hospital treating all kinds of illness takes public patients, unlike a private clinic for paying ones.

clue.text: Expert at unearthing secrets controls fringes of party

indicators.note: fringes are the edges, so the first and last letters are kept

blocks.note: to master is to control
first and last letters of party

explanation.surface: A political fixer runs the edges of a party and digs up its secrets.
explanation.definitionFit: A master spy is a highly skilled espionage agent, someone expert in uncovering hidden information.

clue.text: Dramatic publicity for one who suppresses top jobs?

blocks.note: someone who bans things
head = top, lines = jobs or lines of work

explanation.surface: A censor who stifles senior appointments somehow gets eye-catching publicity.
explanation.walkthrough: BANNER is read as 'one who bans', not a flag; the question mark flags this whimsical split.
explanation.definitionFit: Banner headlines run across the full width of a newspaper's front page, giving a story the most striking possible coverage.

clue.text: Core of estate on Mediterranean, no longer wild

indicators.note: the core is the very centre, so only the middle letters of the word are kept

blocks.note: the two middle letters of the six-letter estate
common short form for the Mediterranean

explanation.surface: The heart of a Mediterranean estate, once wild land, has been brought under control.
explanation.definitionFit: An animal or landscape that has been tamed has been domesticated or subdued, so it is no longer untamed.

clue.text: Ask wrong price as rich gem is exchanged

indicators.note: things exchanged swap places, so these letters trade positions with one another

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A jeweller overcharges when a valuable stone is traded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as' looks like a link word but its two letters belong to the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To mischarge is to bill someone incorrectly, putting an incorrect amount on goods or services.

clue.text: An opening for sarcasm in tough report on MPs

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter, so only that is taken
the earlier pieces go inside the word for tough

blocks.note: tough means hard, difficult
taken as written
first letter of sarcasm

explanation.surface: A harsh parliamentary report leaves room for a sarcastic jibe.
explanation.definitionFit: Hansard is the official verbatim record of debates in the UK Parliament, a report on what MPs say.

clue.text: Stubborn dog, biting one society girl

indicators.note: something biting holds another thing in its jaws, so the dog word encloses the rest

blocks.note: a hound is a dog
the Roman numeral for one
short for debutante, a young woman entering high society

explanation.surface: An obstinate dog bites a young woman at a society ball.
explanation.definitionFit: Hidebound means narrow-minded and set in one's ways, unwilling to change opinions.

clue.text: Spots yours truly at jumble sales

indicators.note: a jumble is a muddle, so the letters of the following word are mixed up

blocks.note: the writer referring to themself
letters of sales rearranged

explanation.surface: The writer browses at jumble sales and notices things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jumble sales' reads as a charity sale, but jumble is the anagram signal. 'Spots' looks like a verb (notices); it is the noun for a rash.
explanation.definitionFit: Measles is an infectious disease whose most visible symptom is a rash of red spots across the skin.

clue.text: US car has series of events as two-wheeler

blocks.note: American word for a car
a recurring series

explanation.surface: An American car goes through a sequence of events and ends up as a bike.
explanation.definitionFit: An autocycle was an early lightweight motorised bicycle, a pedal machine fitted with a small engine.

clue.text: Radical arts CID devised

indicators.note: something devised is newly worked out, so these letters are put into a new order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Detectives come up with a revolutionary scheme for the arts.
explanation.walkthrough: CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, the detective branch of British police.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe measures that are extreme and far-reaching rather than cautious or moderate.

clue.text: After hoax, swimmer could be taken aboard trawler

definitions.note: a descriptive clause rather than a noun: what a trawler might land

blocks.note: a cod is British slang for a hoax or spoof
a fish is a swimmer

explanation.surface: After a prank, a swimmer is hauled onto a fishing boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' tells you the hoax word comes first, with the swimmer following it.
explanation.definitionFit: Trawlers drag nets to catch fish such as cod in large numbers, so a cod is just what one lands.

clue.text: Name worker getting honourable end to slavery

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that is kept

blocks.note: the worker ant is the classic crossword worker
standard abbreviation, as in 'the Hon.'
last letter of slavery

explanation.surface: A labourer is praised for an honourable stand against slavery.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony is a common masculine given name, so it is an example of a name.

clue.text: It measures current strength found in wild mare

indicators.note: wild means untamed and disordered, so the next word's letters are scrambled
the first piece is placed inside the scrambled letters

blocks.note: taken as written before rearranging
to find someone is to meet with them

explanation.surface: A powerful creature is discovered in a wild horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strength' belongs to the definition, not the wordplay: current strength is the amperage measured.
explanation.definitionFit: An ammeter is an instrument that measures electric current in amperes, i.e. how strong the current flowing is.

clue.text: Kind of Bee to lead monk in ways of jobsworths

blocks.note: the bumble-bee is one kind
Dom is a title given to Benedictine and other monks

explanation.surface: A bee guides a monk through the officious habits of petty officials.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to lead' tells you the bee comes first. A jobsworth is British slang for a petty official who sticks to the rules ('more than my job's worth').
explanation.definitionFit: Bumbledom, after Mr Bumble the beadle in Oliver Twist, is self-important petty officialdom and its fussy behaviour.

clue.text: Impudent, like some bigmouth?

blocks.note: first meaning: cheeky, insolent
second meaning, read literally: having large lips

explanation.walkthrough: A bigmouth is usually a loud boaster; the question mark invites reading it as a mouth with big lips.
explanation.definitionFit: Lippy is informal British for cheeky, giving backchat, and literally suggests someone well endowed with lips.

clue.text: Tin holds only one-third of portly fowl

indicators.note: a holder has something inside it, so the tin word wraps the other piece
a third of a six-letter word is two letters, here the opening pair

blocks.note: a tin is a can
first third of portly

explanation.surface: A tin holds a portion of a plump roasting bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A capon is a castrated cockerel fattened for eating, a domestic bird of the poultry kind.

clue.text: Donkey in race gained dynamic energy from carrots

indicators.note: in means inside, so the letters lie within the run of words given

blocks.note: surface padding: sets the scene of a donkey derby
spans the end of gained and the start of dynamic
surface padding: completes the picture of a fed-up runner

explanation.surface: A donkey racer gets a burst of energy from eating carrots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'race', 'energy from carrots' only complete the picture of a donkey derby; they give no letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Neddy is a familiar British name for a donkey, used much as 'moggy' is for a cat.

clue.text: This is acted upon rashly, having no finesse

indicators.note: acting rashly is acting wildly, so the letters before it are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: all fifteen letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone who acts on impulse is shown to lack polish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upon' looks like a joining word but belongs to the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone unsophisticated lacks worldly refinement, polish or subtlety, which is what finesse means.

clue.text: Smart bit of fraud, and yet unprofitable

indicators.note: a bit is a small part, so the letters sit inside the run of words that follows

blocks.note: spans the end of fraud, all of and, and the start of yet
surface padding: the scam that did not pay

explanation.surface: A clever little swindle that still made no money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unprofitable' only completes the picture of a scam that failed to pay; it gives no letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A dandy is a man devoted to fine clothes, and as an adjective it means stylish or excellent.

clue.text: Rough and tumble in staging Equus?

blocks.note: first meaning: boisterous, rowdy fooling about
second meaning, read literally: putting on a stage drama about a stable animal

explanation.walkthrough: Equus is Peter Shaffer's play about a boy who blinds horses, so staging it is putting on a play about equines.
explanation.definitionFit: Horseplay is rowdy, boisterous fooling about, exactly the kind of rough and tumble of children's games.
